(a) Offense.—Chapter 2 of title 18, United States Code, is amended by inserting after section 39 the following:“§ 39A. Aiming a laser pointer at an aircraft“(a) Offense.—Whoever knowingly aims the beam of a laser pointer at an aircraft in the special aircraft jurisdiction of the United States, or at the flight path of such an aircraft, shall be fined under this title or imprisoned not more than 5 years, or both.“(b) Laser Pointer Defined.—As used in this section, the term ‘laser pointer’ means any device designed or used to amplify electromagnetic radiation by stimulated emission that emits a beam designed to be used by the operator as a pointer or highlighter to indicate, mark, or identify a specific position, place, item, or object.“(c) Exceptions.—This section does not prohibit aiming a beam of a laser pointer at an aircraft, or the flight path of such an aircraft, by—“(1) an authorized individual in the conduct of research and development or flight test operations conducted by an aircraft manufacturer, the Federal Aviation Administration, or any other person authorized by the Federal Aviation Administration to conduct such research and development or flight test operations;“(2) members or elements of the Department of Defense or Department of Homeland Security acting in an official 
capacity for the purpose of research, development, operations, testing, or training; or“(3) by an individual using a laser emergency signaling device to send an emergency distress signal.“(d) Authority To Establish Additional Exceptions by Regulation.—The Attorney General, in consultation with the Secretary of Transportation, may provide by regulation, after public notice and comment, such additional exceptions to this section as may be necessary and appropriate. The Attorney General shall provide written notification of any proposed regulations under this section to the Committees on the Judiciary of the Senate and the House of Representatives, the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation of the Senate, and the Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure of the House of Representatives, not less than 90 days before such regulations become final.”
. 
    (b) Clerical Amendment.—The analysis for such chapter is amended—
        (1) by moving the item relating to section 39 after the item relating to section 38; and 
        (2) by inserting after the item relating to section 39 the following:


“39A. 
Aiming a laser pointer at an aircraft”.

fable.w: The tempting reading is that this is only a criminal offense provision whose procedural language stays inside the government, since it has the Attorney General consulting the Secretary of Transportation and notifying congressional committees. Those two features alone would not count. However, subsection (d) authorizes the Attorney General to create additional exceptions by regulation "after public notice and comment," which brings the general public into a federal decision. Rulemaking authority with a public comment period counts as participation even though it is discretionary ("may").
fable.s: The Attorney General, in consultation with the Secretary of Transportation, may provide by regulation, after public notice and comment, such additional exceptions to this section as may be necessary and appropriate.

qwen_block.w: The section explicitly requires 'public notice and comment' before the Attorney General can establish additional exceptions via regulation. This constitutes a public comment period, which is a form of participation involving the general public (outside the federal government) in a federal decision-making process. The consultation with the Secretary of Transportation is intra-governmental and does not count, but the public comment requirement does.
qwen_block.s: The Attorney General, in consultation with the Secretary of Transportation, may provide by regulation, after public notice and comment, such additional exceptions to this section as may be necessary and appropriate.

opus.w: The statute allows the Attorney General to create more exceptions to the laser-pointer offense by regulation, but only 'after public notice and comment.' That is a rulemaking with a public comment period, so people outside the federal government take part in the decision. The consultation with the Secretary of Transportation and the notice to congressional committees stay inside the government and would not count by themselves. The public comment requirement is enough to make the answer Yes.
opus.s: The Attorney General, in consultation with the Secretary of Transportation, may provide by regulation, after public notice and comment, such additional exceptions to this section as may be necessary and appropriate.

**Step 1: Reasoning.** It's tempting to read subsection (d) as purely internal to the government. The Attorney General consults the Secretary of Transportation, which is coordination between federal agencies, and sends notice of proposed rules to congressional committees, which also stays inside the government. Neither of those counts as participation on its own. But the same subsection also says new exceptions may be made only "by regulation, after public notice and comment." Rulemaking with a public comment period brings the general public into a federal decision, so it crosses the federal boundary.
